lines.text: Today you become the boss of your money. You will make a real plan for your pocket money and set up three jars.
Income is the money that comes in, like pocket money, birthday money or a festival gift.
Grown-ups earn their income by working at a job or running a business.
Your income is where every money plan starts.
Spending is the money that goes out when you buy something.
Write down every rupee you spend, even a five rupee toffee.
Small spends add up much faster than you think.
Saving is the money you keep for later.
Pay yourself first: put savings aside as soon as money comes in, not at the end of the week.
Then you will never forget to save.
Split your money into three jars called Spend, Save and Share.
For ₹100, you could put ₹50 in Spend, ₹40 in Save and ₹10 in Share.
Share money can buy a gift for someone or help a good cause.
A budget is a plan that says where each rupee will go before you spend it.
Income minus spending is what is left to save.
If spending is more than income, the plan needs fixing.
Riya gets two hundred rupees of pocket money every week.
As soon as she gets it, she puts sixty rupees in her Save jar and thirty rupees in her Share jar.
That leaves one hundred and ten rupees in her Spend jar for snacks, a notebook and a comic.
One hundred and ten plus sixty plus thirty makes two hundred, so every rupee has a job.
Step one, write down your income for the week.
Step two, list the things you must pay for, like school snacks.
Step three, put your savings and sharing money aside first.
Step four, plan your wants, and step five, check at the end of the week what really happened.
Arjun buys a ten rupee packet of chips every single day.
That does not sound like much, but it is seventy rupees a week.
In a month, it adds up to about two hundred and eighty rupees.
Small daily spends are like a leak in a bucket, so write them down and decide on purpose.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
